Submit
sub-MIT
v.
From Latin submittere, “to place under, lower,” from sub- (under) + mittere (to send, place). Renders the Greek hupotassō, a military term meaning “to arrange under, place in order under,” and the Hebrew kāna, “to humble, be subdued.”

Biblical Definition

To submit is to place oneself in the appointed order under God’s appointed authority—a glad, willing, principled arranging-of-self-under, not a forced subjugation. The Greek hupotassō is a military picture: troops arranged in rank under their commander, each man in his place, the order itself being the means of the army’s strength. Scripture commands a network of such ordered submissions: of all souls to God (submit yourselves therefore to God, Jas 4:7); of the church to Christ; of citizens to civil authorities (Rom 13:1); of believers one to another in the fear of God (Eph 5:21); of wives to their own husbands (Eph 5:22; 1 Pet 3:1); of children to parents (Eph 6:1); of younger to elder in the church (1 Pet 5:5); and of the flock to faithful elders (Heb 13:17). The pattern is not arbitrary hierarchy but ordered relation, by which the household, the church, and the civil order all stand. The supreme model is the Son’s own submission to the Father (1 Cor 15:28), and the Spirit’s ministering to the will of the Son—within an undivided God who is Himself a perfect order of love. Submission is never to be confused with the suppression of personhood, the silencing of conscience before God, or the toleration of sin in the one to whom one is subject; the apostles obey God rather than men when commanded to violate God’s law; the wife does not sin to please her husband; the saint does not bow to civil orders that command idolatry. But within God’s appointed orders and the limits of His Word, submission is the disposition of the Christian heart: a quiet, willing, glad placing of self under, in imitation of the Son and by the strength of the Spirit, for the good of the order, the honor of God, and the flourishing of all whom that order is meant to bless.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SUBMIT as to yield, resign, or surrender to the power, will, or authority of another; to refer; to leave or commit to the discretion or judgment of another.

expand to see more

SUBMIT, v.t. — 1. To let down; to cause to sink or lower. 2. To yield, resign, or surrender to the power, will, or authority of another; to commit. Submit yourselves to your own husbands (Eph 5:22). 3. To refer; to leave or commit to the discretion or judgment of another; as, to submit a controversy to arbitrators.

SUBMIT, v.i. — To surrender; to yield one’s person to the power of another; to give up resistance; to be subject.

Key Scripture

James 4:7 — "Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you."

Ephesians 5:21 — "Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God."

1 Peter 5:5 — "Likewise, ye younger, submit yourselves unto the elder. Yea, all of you be subject one to another, and be clothed with humility..."

Hebrews 13:17 — "Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account."

Modern Corruption

Submission is the most allergic word of the present age, conflated reflexively with abuse and oppression, so that the whole biblical network of ordered submissions—of all to God, of wife to husband, of child to parent, of citizen to magistrate, of saint to elder—is rejected in principle, with grave damage to household, church, and civil order alike.

expand to see more

The age has rendered submission almost unsayable. The word is conflated reflexively with abuse, oppression, suppression of personhood, and the silencing of the weak by the strong; and the whole network of ordered submissions Scripture commands—to God, to Christ, to civil authority, to elders, to husband, to parent—is rejected in principle as inherently demeaning. The result is the systematic disordering of the spheres that God’s appointed submissions are meant to hold together: marriages without a head and without a heart willing to lay itself down; churches in which no flock will be led and no elder is honored; civil society in which authority is presumed illegitimate and disobedience is the default register; and individual souls who have unlearned the very disposition of bowing under, even to God Himself. The pastoral cost is enormous; the cultural cost is greater.

Submission is also corrupted in the opposite direction by the abusive caricature in which submission is treated as servile, unconditional, and total—the wife is to submit to a husband who calls her to sin; the citizen is to obey magistrates ordering idolatry; the church member is to follow elders no matter what they preach. This is not biblical submission; it is the substitution of human tyranny for the ordered relations God commanded. The apostles set the rule: we ought to obey God rather than men. Within God’s orders and the limits of His Word, the saint submits gladly, in imitation of the Son who submitted to the Father; beyond those limits, the same saint stands and bears the consequences. Recover both ends: the principled refusal of every authority that commands sin, and the glad, willing, ordered submission to every authority that does not. The Christian is not a free agent; he is a placed agent—set, like the Son, in the order of His Father’s house.

Hebrew Roots

Greek hupotassō (to arrange under, place in order under)—a military picture of troops in rank—and Hebrew kāna (to humble, be subdued): glad, ordered placing-of-self under God’s appointed authority.

expand to see more

Greek hupotassō (G5293) — to arrange under, subordinate, submit (military origin).

Greek hupotagē (G5292) — the noun: subjection, submission.

Hebrew kāna (H3665) — to humble, bring into subjection.

Hebrew shāphēl (H8213) — to be low, brought down—the humiliation that precedes ordered submission.

Usage

"Submission is the glad placing-of-self under in God’s appointed order—not the suppression of personhood and not the silencing of conscience."

"The supreme model is the Son’s own submission to the Father; the saint’s submissions are imitations of His, in the strength of the same Spirit."

"The age allergic to submission disorders every sphere God’s ordered submissions are meant to hold together—household, church, and civil order alike."
